newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Rising flows pose challenge to Asia bourses - forum.
newsitem.headline: Rising flows pose challenge to Asia bourses - forum.

text.p: Large international capital flows are giving rise to increased volatility in Asian stock markets, and local bourses could limit the impact by promoting domestic investment, experts told a World Economic Forum meeting on Wednesday.

"One of the challenges we are facing are international portfolio investment flows," Edgar Cheng, chairman of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, told a plenary session of the Europe-East Asia Economic Summit.
"They are, in many countries, the main factor determining share price movements," he said.

But moves to control capital flows would be counterproductive and local bourses should work on the depth and liquidity of local capital markets, encouraging the development of domestic mutual fund industries, pension funds and life insurance, he said.
"The overall economic benefits of such (international) flows vastly outweigh any negative side effects," said Cheng.

"I am sure that the volume of cross-border investment will increase...in the coming years and the challenge for the future will be to develop Asian stock markets fast enough to keep up with the international investment flows."

The total market capitalisation of Asia-Pacific stock markets grew to US$5.2 trillion by the end of 1995 from US$3.7 trillion in 1991, said Laura Cha, executive director of the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission.
Asia-Pacific markets now represent 30 percent of global market capitalisation, she said.

Philip Tose, chairman of Peregrine Investments Holdings, said Asian securities markets had grown from "local cartels run by a small group of securities brokers" in the 1980s to professional organisations.
Exchanges should now embrace the "electronic age", he said.
"To me stock exchange floors are dinosaurs...We sit in an electronic age," said Tose, pointing particularly at the Hong Kong stock exchange.
"There is no reason why members of the Hong Kong stock exchange who have offices overseas should not have access 24 hours a day to a trading system" linked directly to the exchange, he said.

The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong introduced a second terminal system in January, allowing brokers to trade from their offices. Cheng said transactions through those terminals currently accounted for almost 50 percent of trading volume.
"Eventually there won't be any floor for a lot of stock exchanges in Asia, including Hong Kong," he said.
